newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Jewish leader tells Swiss to pay Nazi victims now.
newsitem.headline: Jewish leader tells Swiss to pay Nazi victims now.

text.p: The vice-president of the World Jewish Congress urged Switzerland on Monday to pay compensation now to Nazi victims rather than wait for a major report on Swiss financial dealings during the Holocaust.

Greville Janner, a British opposition Labour member of parliament, said Swiss banks and the government should share the cost of an immediate fund in response to allegations that Switzerland profited from the Holocaust.

"If Switzerland wants to be believed that it really intends to make restitution, it will not wait five years. It should make a financial gesture now for the victims of Nazism," Janner told reporters after a day of talks in Berne.

Janner was referring to the setting up of a commission of historians due to be approved by parliament next month. The commission will have up to five years to report on the fate of Jewish wealth and Nazi loot stashed in Switzerland before and during World War Two.

"In my view, it would be very wicked to wait until the end of the commission for any restitution to the victims because by then many of them will be dead and their families will continue to live in poverty," Janner said.

It was the first time a prominent foreign critic had come to Berne to press Swiss leaders and banks for a quick compensation gesture since a wave of allegations that the Swiss hoarded accounts left by Holocaust victims and bought Nazi loot.

Under pressure headed by the World Jewish Congress, Swiss banks agreed to an international commission to oversee a sweep of dormant Holocaust accounts and the government proposed its own commission of independent historians and legal experts.
Janner said he had found no agreement to the creation of an immediate compensation fund in his talks on Monday with Swiss bank representatives and with Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti.
He said, however, that there was some support among Swiss members of parliament whom he also met.
The top Swiss government official in charge of handling the Holocaust allegations said the government had noted Janner's proposal.

But diplomat Thomas Borer said the cabinet's stated policy was to wait for a full report from the historical commission or at least for facts to be established clearly in interim reports, which the commission will be encouraged to make.

"Then the Federal Council (cabinet) will make decisions on any consequences," Borer told a joint news conference with Janner and former British cabinet minister David Hunt, a Conservative member of parliament.
"Our policy is to establish the truth first, in a speedy way," Borer said.
Janner declined to say how much should be in the fund.
"The amount is a matter for the Swiss to decide upon and perhaps to negotiate with the World Jewish Congress and other organisations who look after the victims," he added.

Janner and Hunt also called on Switzerland as well the British, U.S. and other World War Two Allied governments to renegotiate a 1946 deal under which Switzerland paid 250 million Swiss francs in compensation for buying stolen Nazi gold.

Janner has been at the forefront of critics of the 1946 Washington Agreement who say the deal paid Allied countries with gold stolen in part from Jews murdered by the Nazis. Janner wants the money given to Holocaust victims or their heirs.
But Janner said Cotti had repeated Berne's view that the 1946 accord was a valid international treaty freeing it from future claims and cannot be reopened.
